### Chapter 28: Echoes from the Rooftop

The top floor of Gu Enterprises was designed as an exquisite rooftop garden — a zen rock garden with white gravel, neatly trimmed pines, and a full circle of glass railings. Usually it served as a break area for employees, but today it had almost become the place where He Yuwei ended her life.

By the time Lu Ziang and Lin Chuxia arrived, security had already escorted her down to a small meeting room on the 47th floor. He Yuwei sat on the sofa, hair a mess, makeup smeared by tears. She clutched a cup of tea that had long gone cold, looking like a sparrow drenched in the rain.

Lu Ziang pushed the door open, walked slowly to the seat across from her, and sat down. He didn't speak.

The moment He Yuwei saw him, her whole body trembled.

"How did you —"

"I heard you were working here. Thought I'd come see you."

"You're lying." Tears streamed down her face again. "You came to ask me why I was working for Shen Ruyu, didn't you?"

Lu Ziang was silent for a few seconds, then said, "Then tell me. Did she threaten you with your mother's pension?"

He Yuwei's teacup slipped from her hand and hit the carpet with a dull thud, tea soaking a small patch of the floor. Her mouth opened and closed, and her expression crumbled like a dam breaking.

"It wasn't just my mom's pension she threatened me with — she said if I didn't do what she wanted, she'd release the breakup letter I wrote you in college to the public. Your mother never approved of us anyway. If she found out I wrote a letter like that —"

"That letter... I said some horrible things. I said you weren't good enough for me, that a penniless student with no background couldn't match my family — but the truth was, right then my dad had just been diagnosed with cancer, and you were trying to scrape together money for your mom's treatment. I didn't want both pressures crushing you at the same time."

Lin Chuxia, standing at the doorway of the meeting room, froze. This outcome was something she had never anticipated. He Yuwei had been someone carrying burdens for others all along — but no one had ever shared the load with her, including Lu Ziang.

Lu Ziang stood up, walked over beside her, and crouched down. Then he did something no one expected: he put his hand on He Yuwei's head.

"My mom passed away last year. Before she left, she said one thing to me — 'What was that girl's name, your old girlfriend? That young lady was good. When you find someone new, treat her well.'" His voice was very soft. "She never hated you."

He Yuwei sobbed so hard her whole body shook. All those years of guilt she'd been carrying — she could finally let them go.

That night, He Yuwei revealed every instruction Shen Ruyu had given her. What Shen Ruyu wanted was simple: create a hidden backdoor user in Gu Moyan's scheduling system, then push the time and location of internal meetings to an outside source. That way, Shen Ruyu could track Gu Moyan's every move — including private meetings, travel, and the topics of every department meeting.

"What does she want?"

"She wants to force a board vote."

Lin Chuxia took a deep breath. She finally saw the full picture of Shen Ruyu's endgame: by mastering every piece of Gu Moyan's whereabouts, she could preemptively know all his counter-moves on the day of the board meeting — and then use Shen Corporation's nineteen percent equity as leverage to launch a takeover battle for control.

---

**Chapter 29: The Best Defense Is a Good Offense**

"We can't tell Gu Moyan directly. If we do, Shen Ruyu will destroy all the evidence."

Lin Chuxia and Lu Ziang sat in StarTech's office, the entire stack of communication records and timestamps He Yuwei had provided spread out in front of them. Outside the window, the city's most dazzling nightscape sprawled—the financial district's towers stood like a cluster of giant luminous pillars against the dark sky. But they had no appetite for the view.

"Why can't we just tell him?"

"Because—" Lin Chuxia bit her lower lip. "First, Shen Ruyu and Gu Moyan have known each other since childhood. That gives her a built-in 'trustworthy' identity in the Gu family. If Gu Moyan finds out about this, Shen Ruyu will claim it's He Yuwei's word against hers, and then she'll turn around and expose He Yuwei's private life. Your ex-girlfriend would end up getting shattered all over again."

"Second, Shen Ruyu doesn't know we've already mapped out every single timestamp. If I can make her plan 'impossible to execute' before she makes her move—she needs all the minority shareholders on her side to force that board meeting. And minority shareholders only care about profit. So we have to chip away at her coalition, one share at a time."

Lu Ziang looked at her, something gleaming in his eyes.

"You're reminding me of the first time I saw you again. In the conference room, when you wrote that note to Gu Moyan—you weren't complaining about how screwed the situation was. You were already working out a solution."

"Don't flatter me," Lin Chuxia said, rubbing her temples. "Right now I need to figure out how to get those minority shareholders Shen Ruyu recruited to step back to neutral, one by one. Can you dig into a few key people for me—Mr. Zhou from Huayuan Capital, Mr. Sun from Lingnan Industrial, and Mr. Liu, the independent director of the Gu Group? I need to know what projects they're working on right now."

"Give me twelve hours. StarTech's data team is good at this."

He stood to head to the data center and assign tasks, but paused at the door.

"Lin Chuxia, you're juggling three things at once—helping Gu Moyan keep his company, helping He Yuwei escape Shen Ruyu, and your own business analysis. You're trying to be the world's firefighter. Can you really handle all that?"

Lin Chuxia suddenly remembered the system's warning—when her independent affection coefficient passed 60, she'd fall into it uncontrollably. Right now it was 41. Every night she found herself replaying Gu Moyan's expressions, the things he'd said—handing her hot cocoa, asking, "What if you work till dawn and drop dead?" These moments made it harder and harder to treat this "mission" as just a task.

She didn't answer Lu Ziang's question. Instead, she picked up her phone and read Zhao Xiaobei's latest message:

**[Zhao Xiaobei]:** Girl, I swear you're going to ascend one day. Not the cultivation kind—I mean from human to superhero.

Lin Chuxia smiled bitterly and put the phone down. Tribulation or ascension—she couldn't afford to think that far. If the Gu Group's controlling stake got snatched by the Shen family, all her mission progress would reset to zero.

She reopened the system shop. 1000 credits—Mind Reading (Limited Edition). She had 650 now. Needed 350 more.

There was also a hidden prompt in the shop she hadn't seen before:

**[Emergency Mission: Protect Gu Group Control. Time Limit: None—earliest trigger point is the interim board meeting in 28 days. Reward: 1000 credits—the exact amount needed for the Heart of Truth has been reserved for you. Condition: Ensure Gu Moyan receives more than 51% of the supporting votes at the board meeting.]**

**[Note: This mission was auto-generated when the system detected the host's strongest current desire. Protect him, and you protect your own heart.]**

---

Just as Lin Chuxia's corporate battle plan was reaching its most critical phase, an unexpected figure appeared.

Gu Zhenbang—known to all as Old Master Gu, founder of the Gu Group, seventy-two-year-old former chairman, and Gu Moyan's grandfather. He'd returned to Cloud City from his Swiss sanatorium without any warning, without any buildup, as sudden as a summer storm in the middle of a dry month.

The worst part? Shen Ruyu had personally invited him back. She knew about his return even before Gu Moyan did.

The afternoon Old Master Gu walked into the Gu Tower, the entire executive office atmosphere shifted. The usually composed secretaries were all on edge like they were about to take a final exam. Even Team Lead Liu, who was about to retire, put an extra layer of hairspray on his combover.

Lin Chuxia watched from a distance as the old man stepped out of the VIP elevator. He wore a traditional Zhongshan suit and carried a rosewood cane, but his stride was as steady as a man in his sixties. His eyes were as sharp as Gu Moyan's—but more weathered, more worldly, and far less readable.

"Where's Moyan?" Old Master Gu stood in the forty-seventh-floor lobby, scanning the area. Eight attendants stood behind him.

"Old—Old Master Gu, Mr. Gu is out on business—I'll contact him immediately—"

"No need. I'll wait for him here."

Old Master Gu walked straight into the CEO's office and sat in the main chair. He had his attendants close the door behind them.

In the split second before the door shut, Lin Chuxia caught a glimpse through the glass wall of Old Master Gu slowly surveying the room—as if he were seeing everything his grandson had never told him over the years.

An hour later, Lin Chuxia was called into the CEO's office.

Only three people were inside: Old Master Gu, Shen Ruyu—and Gu Moyan, who had just rushed back.

"You're Lin Chuxia?" Old Master Gu leaned back in the executive chair, studying her. "You really do look a bit like that Su family girl."

Lin Chuxia stood still, her heart racing. Even facing Shen Ruyu hadn't made her this nervous—because Old Master Gu carried the kind of oppressive weight that came from a lifetime of seeing through everything, judging only what was real and what was fake.

"Hello, Old Master Gu." She gave a slight bow.

"No need for that. I'm just a retired old man. Nothing to respect." Old Master Gu picked up the Yixing clay teapot from the guest tea table and took a sip. "I came today to ask Moyan three questions."

"First—are you willing to cooperate according to the Shen family's proposal? I've read the proposal Ruyu sent me."

"Second—in your future marriage, how will you ensure the continuation of the Gu bloodline and family legacy?"

"Third—" The old man's gaze shifted from Shen Ruyu to Lin Chuxia, then from Lin Chuxia back to Gu Moyan. "Are you in love with this secretary of yours?"

Three questions in a row. The air in the room compressed into a block of ice.

Shen Ruyu held her teacup and smiled faintly, looking down—this was the chess move she'd prepared all along. Inviting the old man back was her way of using his authority to force Gu Moyan into a corner. If Gu Moyan dared to defend Lin Chuxia in front of his grandfather, he would be unfilial. If he went along with Old Master Gu's wishes, Lin Chuxia would be out of the picture.

But she had miscalculated one thing.

"Grandfather," Gu Moyan spoke, his voice steady as a mountain. "First question—I don't want to cooperate under the Shen family's terms because the Shen family has contributed no intangible assets to the Gu Group. Second question—family legacy can be secured through corporate bylaws; there's no need to gamble on marriage. As for the third—"

He turned and faced Lin Chuxia. Then he said it to everyone in the room.

"Yes. I love her. Not because she looks like someone else."

---

Old Master Gu fell silent for a long time.

His rosewood cane tapped the carpet three times—tap, tap, tap. It was his thinking habit. Everyone in the room froze. Shen Ruyu's teacup hovered in midair. Lin Chuxia's breath went on mute.

Then the old man stood up and walked over to Lin Chuxia. He wasn't tall, but when he looked up at someone, there was a commanding presence. His voice was old and steady, like a ruler that had been overused but never bent.

"You're Lin Chuxia. Orphanage raised, full scholarship to Cloud City University. In one year at Gu Group, you've written more detailed analysis reports than some of the veterans in the secretarial office who've been there for over a decade."

"I looked into you—before you came to see me."

He leaned on his cane and walked to the floor-to-ceiling window, gazing out at Cloud City. The sunlight stretched his shadow long across the floor.

"A little girl with nothing, using her own wits to hold off two generations of pressure from the Shen family in the business world. You protected my grandson three times—first with the safety hazard at Huaxing Real Estate, second with the brand damage at the charity gala, and third with the Shen family's minority shareholder alliance that's still being dismantled piece by piece. You've done all that without asking for anything in return. Have you?"

Lin Chuxia didn't speak. The system behind her was frantically scanning Old Master Gu's emotional data, but she herself just wanted to listen to this conversation fully.

"No, I thought so." The old man turned to face Shen Ruyu. "Ruyu—I really liked the way you used to come over and play at our house when you were little. But business is business, and feelings are feelings. If the Shen family wants to take down the Gu Group, go ahead on the battlefield of commerce. Within the rules, I won't protect anyone. But if you keep treating my grandson as leverage for your Shen family's marriage alliance—"

He lightly stamped his cane on the floor.

"Don't forget that I, Gu Zhenbang, am still alive in Cloud City."

Shen Ruyu's face went pale beneath her flawless makeup. She had never been treated like this by the elder who had doted on her for decades. She stood up, said "Old Master Gu, please rest," and walked out quickly.

But the expression on her face as she exited didn't escape Lin Chuxia's eyes. Shen Ruyu was only suppressed here by an elder she couldn't defy, but her game wasn't lost. She would just switch to a more covert tactic.

Old Master Gu sat back down in his chair and looked at Lin Chuxia. "Young lady, I have only one question for you."

"Please ask."

"If someday the Gu Group no longer needs you to guard it for him, where do you want to go?"

Lin Chuxia thought for a moment and told the truth. "I don't know. I've never thought about 'the day I'm no longer needed.' Because I'm staying by his side—not to be needed by him."

"Then why?"

"Because during the time I've been with him—" She searched for the right words and chose the most honest phrasing. "It's been the most fulfilling period of my life. Not because of who he is, but because in everything I've done, I've been becoming a better version of myself."

The old man looked at her for a long time. Finally, he stood up and walked toward the office door. As he passed Gu Moyan, he patted his shoulder.

"Good pick this time," he murmured, low enough that only Gu Moyan could hear—but Lin Chuxia still caught it.

Old Master Gu's assistant opened the door for him, and the old man, leaning on his cane, stepped into the elevator. After he left, the air in the office felt like a coiled spring that had been wound tight for half a century, suddenly released.

---

After seeing Old Master Gu out, Gu Moyan returned to his office alone, loosened his tie, then grabbed his car keys and called for Lin Chuxia.

"Come with me. We're going somewhere—not a cemetery."

Twenty minutes later, the car pulled up in front of a very humble noodle shop. Not a Michelin-starred restaurant. Not a private club. Just a small Chongqing-style noodle shop tucked away in an old alley, with a rusty wind chime by the door and plastic tables and chairs that looked like they’d been through a generation.

"This place was my mom's," Gu Moyan said after he sat down, aligning the chopsticks on the table.

Lin Chuxia froze. In all the character introductions from the original novel, the only information about Gu Moyan's mother was four words: "Gu's mother deceased."

"She wasn't some highborn lady. She was just the owner of this little noodle shop from Chongqing. When my dad wanted to marry her, he had a full-blown fight with the entire Gu family." Gu Moyan picked up the chili jar and added two spoonfuls of red oil—he'd started embracing the Sichuan heat since that meal at the private kitchen with her.

"So the old man isn't really against me choosing a girl from a humble background. What pissed him off wasn't 'I won't marry Shen Ruyu,' it was that he took the same path for my mom back then—he made the same choice, and now I'm walking it again. He's scared I'll pay the same price."

He said it all matter-of-factly, but she could read the unspoken words behind what came next.

"My parents died in a car crash when I was thirteen."

Lin Chuxia's fingers unconsciously tightened on the table. She looked at him—a boy who'd lost his parents at thirteen, who'd grown up under the crushing weight of a family like the Gus without them, and in sixteen years had become the most powerful voice in the city's business circles.

And now he was sitting in the noodle shop his mother used to run, pushing a bowl toward her.

"Try the pea-and-pork noodles here. Her—my mom's recipe hasn't changed much," he said, his eyes a little wet beneath the warm yellow light of the shop, but his voice steady. "When I was a kid, I'd come here after school and sit right here—this exact spot. I'd do my homework while she'd put a bowl in front of me and yell at me for how ugly my handwriting was."

She bent her head and took a bite. The noodles were fiery, the aroma of chili oil rushing straight up her nose, and the tears mixed with emotion until she couldn't tell which was fueling which.

"Thank you," he said.

"For what?"

"That day at the cemetery—you asked me a question, didn't you? 'Are you looking for a substitute to punish her or to punish yourself?' No one had ever asked me that. Not my therapist. Not my grandfather. Everyone thought Gu Moyan didn't need to be questioned. But that one kept me up for a long time."

He took a sip of the broth, then looked at her and spoke for the third time.

"Lin Chuxia—before you, I wasn't afraid of losing anyone. Because I'd accepted loss as normal. Mom left. Dad left. Wanqing left. But that night, when you stayed late at the office until dawn, and I watched your back in the elevator—"

"I realized I was scared. Scared that you might vanish too. The way I'm scared that a bowl of noodles will go cold before I finish it."

The system panel showed the affinity rating flickering. But she turned it off. She didn't want to reduce this moment to a number.

---

After Old Master Gu publicly berated her, Shen Ruyu finally quieted down for a few days. But Lin Chuxia knew that Shen Ruyu's silence wasn't surrender—she was regrouping.

Sure enough, three days later, an internal company announcement went out: the Gu Corporation would hold an emergency board meeting next Wednesday. The agenda? Adjustments to the company's strategic direction.

Lin Chuxia called He Yuwei. "Did Shen Ruyu ask you to download all the files she needs to an external hard drive during the day after tomorrow's system maintenance window—you know, that two-hour period when the whole company system goes offline for updates?"

He Yuwei was silent on the line for a moment before saying something hard to believe.

"Sister Chuxia—actually, that day I went up to the rooftop, it wasn't to jump."

"What do you mean?"

"That day I did stand by the railing. But I was waiting for someone."

"For who?"

"Shen Ruyu told me to go to the rooftop at 3 PM that day—she would give me something to get rid of the threat. But the security guard came up too early, and she never showed. The moment you pushed open the meeting room door, I realized: while I was standing up there, she was probably watching from far below, waiting for me to completely break down in front of everyone. That way, I wouldn't be seen as a 'snitch'—I'd just look mentally unstable."

Lin Chuxia felt her blood boil. Shen Ruyu had never planned to let He Yuwei leave peacefully. She wanted to push He Yuwei to a breaking point, then fire her under the pretext of 'the CEO's secretary is mentally unstable.' And throughout it all, Shen Ruyu's hands stayed clean.

"So what do you want to do now?" Lin Chuxia asked.

"Sister Chuxia, I want to win." He Yuwei's voice no longer trembled. "After spending these days with you and Lu Ziang, one thought has become clearer and clearer: Shen Ruyu was able to control me for so long not because she was so powerful—but because I felt I wasn't good enough, that I didn't deserve protection."

"And now?"

"Now I think I can turn that maintenance window against her—right there in those two hours when the whole company system goes offline the day after tomorrow."

Lin Chuxia listened quietly as He Yuwei laid out her plan. That girl was actually very smart—she had just been crushed by fear before. She proposed an extremely bold scheme: during the maintenance window, exploit the permissions design of the Gu Corporation system update mechanism to automatically generate an unalterable security log of all unauthorized external access records, and send it simultaneously to the corporate email of every board member.

Wednesday at 9 AM—one hour before the emergency board meeting—Shen Ruyu would be facing evidence that all thirty-plus board members would see together.

"Can you handle this alone?"

"I've already coordinated with the IT department in advance," He Yuwei said. "They've been suspicious about the Shen family's unauthorized data access for a while. The IT people said—if anyone tries anything during the maintenance window, their security system will generate a detailed, complete record immediately."

Lin Chuxia hung up and looked out the window.

Cloud City was suddenly hit by a rainstorm. The sky turned dark and oppressive, like the eerie calm three minutes before a downpour.

---

Saturday evening. A fine rain fell over Cloud City. Beneath the streetlights, the droplets glittered like countless strands of silver thread.

Lu Ziang stood with an umbrella outside a small tea shop by Houhai. He Yuwei faced him, the seven years between them and a breakup letter forming an invisible wall.

"Seeing you pour everything into protecting Gu Moyan's company—it reminded me of the way you helped me with my thesis back in college," Lu Ziang said, tilting his umbrella toward her. His own shoulder was getting soaked.

"You're still the same—helping others until you're the one getting wet." Her eyes reddened, but she didn't cry.

"I never blamed you for writing that farewell letter. My mom's surgery back then cost thirty thousand. I was already hesitating about whether to tell you I had no money. I backed out first. You just gave me an out before I could."

He Yuwei dropped her gaze. Rain dripped from her chin—impossible to tell if it was tears or rainwater.

"After we parted ways on Wednesday, I thought a lot," she said, looking up at him. "The reason I never dated in these seven years... It wasn't because I couldn't get over you." She paused. "It's because after the breakup, I couldn't face myself. I was afraid I was the kind of person who runs away when things get hard."

Lu Ziang handed her the umbrella and stepped back into the rain. Water slid from his hair, but he smiled—that same warm smile from college. Not for show. Genuine.

"Your first run doesn't define you forever. And on Wednesday, you didn't run."

"No—Wednesday I didn't run. I stood in the server room, staring at the monitor as I typed those access commands. My hands were shaking, but my mind was clear. In that moment, I knew—the old He Yuwei was still there. But she doesn't need you to hold an umbrella for her anymore."

Lu Ziang stood in the rain watching her. After a long moment, he took the umbrella back. This time, he held it squarely over his own head.

The two walked from the little tea shop by Houhai all the way to the subway station. Most of the walk was in silence. But when they parted, Lu Ziang watched her back, and that tangled knot of old feelings inside him slowly came loose.

---

**Chapter 35: A Heart Takes Root in the Chest**

Wednesday morning, the last few hours before the Gu Group's interim board meeting.

Lin Chuxia sat in her 42nd-floor office, staring at a long-cold cup of black coffee. The business side was all in place—He Yuwei's security logs, Gu Moyan's countermeasures, and the business synergy strategy she'd seen in the system's prophecy book. Every piece was on the board. Twenty-four hours from now, Shen Ruyu's game would be checkmated.

But none of that was on her mind right now.

What she was thinking about was what Gu Moyan had said at the noodle shop: "I'm afraid you'll disappear too—the same way I'm afraid a bowl of noodles will go cold."

She opened the system panel and looked at the numbers she'd been tracking for months.

Gu Moyan affection: 51. Mid-crush stage. A long way from her initial "negative twenty." Her own independent affection coefficient: 49. Not synced.

Eleven points to go. Once her independent affection passed 60, with or without the system, she would truly love this man.

But as she sat in her office reviewing everything, she realized it wasn't about completing a task anymore. Not since he folded that tissue neatly into his suit pocket at the cemetery. Not since he stood by the chili jar at the noodle shop, frowning from the spice but refusing to say a word. Not since he worked late into the night, put a hot cocoa in front of her, and asked, "What happens if you drop dead from exhaustion?"

She knew she'd have to face a question sooner or later.

And she'd saved it for today.

She took the elevator to the 47th floor, passed through the glass doors of the reception area, and walked to the president's office door. He Yuwei sat at her desk outside, giving Lin Chuxia a complicated but sincere look of encouragement.

"President Gu, can I go over the last part of yesterday's proposal with you?"

"Come in."

He was sitting behind his desk, looking at something—not a document, not his phone, but a small paper invitation. It was a family dinner invitation sent by Old Master Gu's secretary: seven o'clock, at the old mansion where he lived. The invitees included Gu Moyan—and Lin Chuxia.

She turned the invitation over. On the back was a personal inscription from Old Master himself: "No business talk. Just ask the young lady once: if you ever got separated from the Gu family, where would you go back to?"

"Should we go tonight?" she asked.

Gu Moyan stood up and walked over to her. His glacial face wore an expression she'd never seen before—not tenderness, not hesitation—but a pure, stripped-down gaze, like standing in the eye of a storm where all strategy and calculation had been abandoned.

He reached out, gently wiped the corner of her mouth with his thumb—she had a little coffee stain from drinking earlier. The motion was light, but the warmth of his touch lingered.

"Chuxia." He said her name without adding "Secretary Lin."

Her ears turned bright red like boiled shrimp. Her temperature spiked. The system flashed Affection +2, +2, +2 beside her—but she couldn't focus on a single number.

"I had a preparatory meeting this morning about board control," he said. "I'm ready with the shares, the business rules, everything. But—"

"I don't think I know how to love someone. I haven't faced this in thirteen years. I need someone to tell me what I should and shouldn't do right now."

She set the invitation back on the desk and looked up at him.

"You can start by not working until 2:30 in the morning by yourself."

He smiled. It was a glimmer of light from deep in his eyes—not the all-around, polished smile of business transactions. It was the smile of "there's someone watching."

---

## Chapter 36: The Old Master’s Gate

At 6:50 in the evening, a black Maybach rolled through the gates of the Gu family’s old mansion in Cloud City’s eastern outskirts.

It wasn’t the sprawling compound you’d expect. Instead, it was a modest three-courtyard home, quiet and elegant. An osmanthus tree stood in one corner of the yard, its branches still. Moss clustered in the cracks between the bluestone paving. Warm yellow light spilled through carved wooden windows, pooling across the stones.

Old Master Gu sat in a rosewood armchair in the main hall, a charcoal stove warming a pot of wine beside him. The scent of osmanthus blossom liquor filled the room.

“Sit. None of that Gu-family formal crap tonight—it’s just the three of us.” He waved a hand, and the old family servant quietly withdrew.

Dinner was a spread of home-style dishes: steamed sea bass, sweet-and-sour ribs, a wood ear mushroom salad, and a pot of free-range chicken soup that had been simmering all afternoon. No five-star chef—Old Master Gu had slow-cooked everything himself in the small kitchen. Leaning on his cane, he sat at the table and personally ladled Lin Chuxia a bowl of soup.

“Little girl, I took a good look at that proposal you gave Moyan this afternoon. ‘Using tech integration to replace a stock battle’—solid thinking. Long-term. Not like those young punks in the boardroom who only know how to fight for votes.”

“Thank you, Old Master.”

“That wasn’t a compliment.” He sipped his own soup, unhurried, then set the bowl down with calm authority. “I invited you tonight to talk business—well, no. You two together know more about that than a retired old man like me. What I want to ask is something else.”

Lin Chuxia put down her chopsticks.

“I’ll put it to you like this: tomorrow, the board vote goes through, the Gu Group stabilizes, and Moyan’s fifty-one percent is locked in. Then, one day, you leave this company. You leave his side. Where do you want to go?”

This was the sequel to their earlier conversation in the office. Old-school people never say everything at once.

Lin Chuxia thought for a moment, then told the truth. “I haven’t planned to leave. But if I did—I’d probably try being a business consultant. Specializing in helping young people who fight their way up in the corporate world. The ones like me—kids who grew up in orphanages—find their core competitive edge.”

Old Master Gu was silent for a long time. The candle flame flickered twice on the table.

“And if Moyan wants to marry you—are you truly ready to step into the Gu family? Your business skills are solid, but the Gu family’s door—” He looked out the window at the old osmanthus tree. “Coming in is easy. Leaving is easy, too. The hard part is living your whole life under everyone’s gaze.”

Gu Moyan’s chopsticks, reaching for a dish, paused for the briefest fraction of a second.

Lin Chuxia seized that beat.

“I never planned to ‘step into the Gu family.’ I just happened to fall in love with your grandson. And your grandson just happens to be part of the Gu family.”

The old man looked at her for a long moment. Then he let out three loud peals of laughter—so forceful that osmanthus petals fluttered down from the tree.

“You little rascal,” he said to Gu Moyan, “this time, your taste is better than your grandfather’s back in the day.” He raised his osmanthus wine glass and clinked it against Gu Moyan’s.

That meal stretched late into the night. When they stepped outside, moonlight painted the bluestone path, and Lin Chuxia’s heels clicked crisply against the stones. Gu Moyan walked on her left, his arm close but not touching. A few osmanthus petals had drifted into her hair.

He stopped.

“Don’t move—there’s a petal in your hair.”

She stood still, her heart hammering against her ribs. He picked the petals out of her hair, one by one—slowly, deliberately, as if stretching out the moment. Moonlight slipped through the leaves and spilled over them.

“There. Done.” A pause. “But—there’s one I’m keeping.”

“Wh—why?”

“Because then I’ll have an excuse to keep looking at you.”

---

**Chapter 37: Shen Ruyu's Final Trump Card**

Wednesday morning, 7:00 AM. Two and a half hours until the emergency board meeting.

A knock at Lin Chuxia's apartment door. She opened it to find an unexpected visitor—Shen Ruyu.

Shen Ruyu looked nothing like her usual self today. No makeup. Her hair pulled back in a simple ponytail. She wore plain white athletic clothes, with deep dark circles under her eyes. In her hand, she held a manila envelope.

"Can we talk inside?"

Lin Chuxia stepped aside.

Shen Ruyu sat down on the couch and placed the envelope on the coffee table. Her voice was calm, but beneath that calm was the cold, calculated danger of someone backed into a corner.

"I didn't trigger any alerts during yesterday's maintenance window. You had He Yuwei change the permissions in advance, didn't you?"

Lin Chuxia didn't deny it.

"Not just the permissions," she confessed. "He Yuwei linked all unauthorized external access records to your backend account. Yesterday afternoon, every board member received an auto-generated security report. Every single detail of your tampering with Gu Moyan's schedule management system was in that email."

Shen Ruyu closed her eyes for a moment. She fumbled in her bag for a cigarette, but glanced around Lin Chuxia's apartment and didn't light it.

"So I've already lost at the board meeting. No votes, no moral high ground, and even He Yuwei slipped out of my control."

"You were never going to win," Lin Chuxia said. "It's not that you didn't have enough tricks. It's because you've always treated Gu Moyan's marriage as a business asset. But he's a living, breathing person. You never even bothered to see who he really is."

"I know exactly who he is," Shen Ruyu's voice finally wavered. "I've known him since I was six. For years after his mother passed, he barely spoke. He'd hide behind the garage after school and cry alone. Back then, the cloth shoes his mother had made for him—he wore them until his toes poked through, but he couldn't bear to throw them away."

Lin Chuxia fell silent.

"I didn't want to treat him as a business asset. I was raised with those four words drilled into me: 'Gu family daughter-in-law.' Do you think I wanted to be the villain? My father told me from childhood: 'If you can't marry into the Gu family, the Shen family real estate will be swallowed up.' All my pride, all my scheming, all those vicious tactics you condemn—they're just the scars I earned trying to survive in a game where everything revolved around one person."

Lin Chuxia was quiet for a long moment before speaking: "Did you ever tell him any of this?"

For the first time, Shen Ruyu's voice cracked with real tears. "How could I tell him? What was I supposed to say—'Hey, Gu Moyan, I've been preparing for you like the national college entrance exam since I was a kid. One false move and it's all over'?"

Lin Chuxia picked up the envelope from the coffee table and opened it. Inside was a letter of intent for equity transfer—a portion of Shen Ruyu's personal shares in the Gu Group would be unconditionally transferred to a charitable trust called the 'Gu Employee Education Fund.' The principal's signature line was blank. The trustee field was also empty.

"This is my last card," Shen Ruyu said as she stood up. "I'm giving it to the Gu Group—but not for Gu Moyan. It's for you. You won—not because you outplayed me, but because you dared to choose him in front of people who never would."

---

**Chapter 38: The Weight of the Boardroom**

At nine thirty in the morning, the 48th floor of Cloud Tower, headquarters of the Gu Group.

The twelve-meter African mahogany conference table sat in a room where all twenty board seats were filled. The atmosphere hung like a frozen block of ice—a chill perfectly calibrated to corporate indifference, every face wearing that practiced expression of "I know everything but I'm showing nothing."

Gu Moyan sat at the head. To his left was Old Master Gu's representative seat—empty, but with the old man's rosewood cane placed across it. To his right sat Shen Jianguo.

Lin Chuxia attended as Strategic Advisor for Corporate Social Responsibility. Her seat was in the observer area, but her gaze connected—subtly, deliberately—with at least four people in the room: Gu Moyan; Lu Ziang (CEO of Stellar Tech, attending as an independent technical advisor); He Yuwei, standing outside in the hallway; and Zhao Xiaobei, who had somehow finagled a remote observer slot under the dubious title "IT Support Liaison."

Gu Moyan opened the meeting.

"First item on today's agenda: the 'Strategic Direction Adjustment' proposal submitted by Shen's Real Estate."

Shen Jianguo spoke with the unhurried, measured cadence he always used.

"Fellow directors, as the Gu Group's partner of nineteen years and its second-largest shareholder, Shen's Real Estate has always held a deep concern for the long-term future of this company. The adjustment we propose is not a vote against President Gu's leadership. Rather, it is a recommendation to incorporate professional real estate management expertise at the core decision-making level."

"And by 'professional real estate management expertise'—" Lu Ziang cut in, "you mean the kind where you knew about the interest bindings with three minority shareholders before anyone else did?"

Around the room, board members shifted uncomfortably. Lu Ziang pulled up a projection, displaying a tripartite agreement between Huayuan Capital's President Zhou, Lingnan Industry's President Sun, and Shen's Real Estate. The clauses clearly outlined an interest-alliance structure Shen's Real Estate had built through commercial tactics.

Sweat beaded on Shen Jianguo's forehead.

"The source of this data—"

"Comes from public filings in China's business registry," Lin Chuxia interjected, her voice steady, like a lecturer guiding a class. "Under the rules for public disclosure of corporate transactions, any agreement involving changes to shareholding must be filed with the business credit information system within fifteen working days of signing. Your cooperation agreements with those three companies were archived with the commerce department last month. Anyone can access them for a fee."

The room fell into a dead silence.

When the voting results for Shen Jianguo's shareholder resolution came in, every eye locked onto the count screen. Total support for Gu Moyan's team: fifty-nine percent. Shen's proposal was rejected.

As the board meeting adjourned, Shen Jianguo walked past Lin Chuxia on his way out. He didn't speak, but he paused for a single beat.

After he left, Lin Chuxia found a small card under her meeting notes. There was only one line on it: "Give the one in the envelope to you — don't mention the other one I gave to Gu Moyan."

Lin Chuxia remembered Shen Ruyu's words that morning on the couch—how she'd placed a share transfer document in the charitable trust. And another one, slipped into Gu Moyan's desk drawer before she left, with a note that read: "To him from 6 years old."

The little girl who had known him since she was six was, at the moment the game was ending, leaving her final wager on the protagonist's table.

---

After the board meeting, the executive floor on the 47th was as quiet as a beach after the tide receded. The crowd had dispersed, the files were put away. The residual heat of the battle settled slowly onto every marble floor tile lit by the afternoon sun in Cloud Tower.

Gu Moyan sat alone behind his desk, holding the envelope Shen Ruyu had left in his drawer. The envelope was old-fashioned—thin paper, edges faintly yellowed, the ink a deep blue from a fountain pen.

He didn't open it. He just turned it over in his hands for a long time. Then he called Lin Chuxia in.

"Shen Ruyu gave the group an employee education fund, with the trustee signature left blank—I understand that part. But what does this mean, giving it to you?" He pushed the envelope toward her, showing her the line on the front.

Lin Chuxia walked over and stood beside him. She relayed the gist of their conversation that morning.

Gu Moyan was silent for a long time.

"She said she prepared for you since you were young like the college entrance exam—she couldn't afford a single mistake."

"And then?" He looked up at her. It wasn't an accusation. It was a voice of deep confusion finally being untangled.

"So I don't think she's a bad person. She was just too tired."

Gu Moyan opened the letter. Inside were two sheets of paper.

The first was a children's drawing, folded in thirds and smoothed flat. Two little people holding a dog. At the bottom right, in crooked handwriting, three characters: Moyan-ge. The edges were creased countless times, deeply worn, but the paper itself was still pristine—kept with care.

The second sheet was a handwritten note in a grown-up's pen:

"I put this drawing in your drawer. With it goes all my memories of you from when I was six.

You don't have to forgive me, but I want to give this to you—because when I was six, all I wanted was to play with you. That was the you I loved most in my whole life."

Gu Moyan stared at the drawing for a long time. The sunlight outside the window slowly shifted direction. The eyes that usually betrayed nothing were, in that moment, soft.

"She drew this when she was six. I was eight. She spent an entire afternoon on it—and then we taped it to the doorframe of Grandpa's study. When we moved, it got torn off. I never found it. She never said anything. Twenty-one years—I thought it was gone forever."

He looked down at the crooked big characters—almost as if he could hear her holding it up, saying, "Look—I drew this for you!"

After a long moment, they left the office. On the hallway, He Yuwei passed by with a box of files and stole a glance at him. She saw him carefully fold the drawing and slip it into the inside chest pocket of his suit before he reached the elevator.

---

On Saturday afternoon, in the commercial district of downtown Cloud City. Zhao Xiaobei and Lin Chuxia each clutched an extra-large bubble tea, sitting on a bench in the middle of the mall, watching the crowd drift by with nothing better to do.

Zhao Xiaobei had lost weight over the past few months—nearly six months of high-pressure torture in Gu Corp's marketing department—but somehow she looked more energetic than ever. The source of her energy was simple: the people who used to look down on her now invited her for coffee, eager to learn her social media strategies.

"Girl, you're the hottest person in the whole company," Zhao Xiaobei said, taking a sip. "No, the hottest person in the entire Cloud City business circle—'the mysterious female strategic advisor who saved Gu Corp's control as a secretary and brokered the tech partnership with StarTech.' Several big finance accounts wanted to interview you, but your new assistant on the 42nd floor turned them all down."

"I have an assistant?"

"You didn't know? HR assigned her to your department last week. Xiao He recommended her—a recent graduate from the administrative institute, really sharp and efficient."

Lin Chuxia felt a little dazed. It had been nearly a year since she came to this world. From starting with a -20 favorability score, to taking on Shen Ruyu's system step by step, to last night under the osmanthus tree at the old family mansion—she had gone from a stand-in forced to follow the original storyline to someone truly seen by this world.

"And you?" Lin Chuxia asked Zhao Xiaobei.

"I got an offer from StarTech." Zhao Xiaobei said it casually, but Lin Chuxia knew she was deliberately downplaying it.

"What position?"

"Director of New Media. Lu Ziang said—" She bit into a tapioca pearl, drawing out the word. "He said he saw the social data report I did for Gu Corp over six months, and his conclusion was that if I stayed at Gu Corp another year—I'd work myself into an early grave."

"So what are you thinking?"

"I'm going. Not because the pay is better—okay, it is better—but mainly because I like building new things. Gu Corp is good, but it's too slow. One idea has to go through seven rounds of approval—by the time it gets approved, your creative heart has already flatlined."

Lin Chuxia watched her, listened to her, and remembered that weekend the two of them shared duck intestines at a Chongqing-style hotpot place—back when they were both in a "just surviving at this company would be amazing" state. Now they were both on the best upward trajectory of their lives.

The afternoon sunlight streamed down through the mall's glass dome. The melting tapioca pearls in their bubble tea looked like stars fallen into their cups.

"Chuxia."

"Hmm?"

"If one day you decide to leave, will you walk away cleanly? Or will you leave something behind on someone that can't be untied?"

Lin Chuxia didn't answer. Because she had too many things she couldn't untie left in this city. Not just one person. Not just one thing.

"I don't know."

"It's okay—" Zhao Xiaobei tossed her empty cup into the trash can. "All the 'I don't knows' are foreshadowing for the future."

---

**Chapter 41: The Undercurrents of a New Track**

*Ding — Main Storyline Quest Released: Signing of the Business Collaboration Agreement. Objective: Facilitate the signing of a joint laboratory cooperation framework agreement between Gu Group and StarTech. Time limit: Two weeks. Success reward: 600 points + hidden item "Future Industry Blueprint Vol. II." Failure penalty: The cooperation opportunity will be permanently closed.*

Lin Chuxia stared at the quest notification that had popped up the moment she woke up, her mental gears already turning.

She wasn't surprised by the joint lab direction — the second strategy in the business prophecy book had made it clear. But the two-week deadline was tight: the competitive relationship between the two companies, the legal department's review process, plus the approvals needed from both sides' investors and board of directors — any one of these could drag the timeline past the failure point.

She immediately opened her laptop and started organizing the proposal. She'd been building this plan on and off for over two months — ever since that night when Gu Moyan told her to "elaborate on that second suggestion" during overtime. The information was about ninety percent complete — still missing a core piece of data from StarTech: their estimated technology investment for the joint lab, plus the initial framework for intellectual property sharing boundaries.

She called Lu Ziang.

"I was just about to reach out — this call of yours beat me to it," Lu Ziang's voice came through, accompanied by the scratching sound of his pen on paper in the background.

"I need your tech investment estimates and IP sharing framework — can you have it ready by this weekend?"

"I have an AI summit to attend tomorrow and the day after — but I'll finish the remaining parts of the document during the half-day drive tomorrow afternoon. I should be able to send you a complete version by Friday. But let me warn you," his tone shifted into serious business negotiation mode, "some of StarTech's investors are very sensitive about Gu Group's 'original sin.' I might need you to come talk to them in person — as a partner, not a secretary."

"No problem."

She hung up and spun a couple of times in her office chair. The system had pushed out another update while she was sleeping last night — her Independent Affection stat was now at 55. Just five points away from that number she both craved and feared: 60.

Her phone buzzed.

【Zhao Xiaobei】: Major find. Remember that shareholder you asked me to look into — Sun Yifan, son of Sun Lao from Lingnan Industries? His wife's company's cooperation agreement with Shen's Real Estate expires next week.

【Lin Chuxia】: How did you find that?

【Zhao Xiaobei】: I'm in the data team at my new company now — this is a legitimate public competitive analysis. I got IT to approve some overtime for me to dig into it. You owe me hotpot.

Lin Chuxia quickly mapped this timeline into her plan — one of the wife's companies was running an AI education project, pure traditional industry. If she could match that business with the joint lab's technology... Old Sun was already leaning away from the Shen family in board meetings anyway.

All the threads were slowly converging.

She set her phone down on the desk and gazed at Cloud City's skyline through the window. She'd seen this view countless times, but today, with the sunlight streaming in from this particular angle, she suddenly felt something shift. She no longer had the panic of her early days here, that desperate feeling of "I have to rely on the system to take the next step." Not because she had enough points, but because she understood the chessboard well enough now that she no longer needed to ask the system.

---

It was Zhao Xiaobei's third week at StarTech when Lin Chuxia invited her to meet at their usual spot—the same hotpot restaurant, the same table by the window. The bubbling red oil broth was loaded with Sichuan peppercorns and dried chilies, filling the air with that unmistakable Chongqing hotpot aroma.

"So? Is the new job living up to your expectations?"

Zhao Xiaobei put down her chopsticks and gave Lin Chuxia a look that said, "I have something huge to tell you." "Girl—I finally understand what it means to have a comfortable kind of grind."

"What do you mean?"

"I mean—your workload is still huge, but you don't have to waste half your energy dealing with office politics. There are twelve people on our team. Ten of them are focused on the product. Zero of them are figuring out how to stab a coworker in the back. Zero! You know, for the first time in my career, I don't have to come in with my defenses up. If someone opposes your proposal in a meeting, it's not because they're out to get you—it's because they genuinely think the plan could be better."

"You've got PTSD from dealing with those goody-two-shoes at Gu Group." Lin Chuxia smiled and picked up a piece of beef tripe for her.

"I'm serious. Lu Ziang is a solid boss—of course, you already knew that before I did—but I'm not just talking about him being a nice guy. His management logic is crystal clear: I hired you to do a job, so I give you the resources, the authority, and the pay you deserve, and then I stay the hell out of your way. If you do well, I acknowledge it. If you screw up, we regroup together."

"So what's his flaw?"

Zhao Xiaobei thought for a moment. "He's too warm. To everyone—colleagues, partners, everyone. You can never tell if he has a special person in his life, or if he's just that nice to the whole world. That's both his biggest strength and his biggest weakness."

Lin Chuxia thought of the favorability mark on the system—43—and let out a soft sigh.

"By the way, has He Yuwei been in contact with him lately?" Zhao Xiaobei asked.

"Yeah. The two of them seem to have reconnected a bit—not getting back together, but at least they're able to be friends again. He Yuwei went to StarTech's AI education project last week to volunteer as a helper."

"You know what? I had coffee with He Yuwei once. She's so happy every day now. Not because she has a boyfriend—she doesn't—but because she finally feels like she's gotten past her fears." Zhao Xiaobei drained the last of her sour plum drink. "I'd rather be her friend by about ten thousand times than be Shen Jiajia's coworker."

"Do you have a boyfriend?" Lin Chuxia suddenly asked.

Zhao Xiaobei nearly choked. "Why are you asking me that out of nowhere?! I'm so busy I don't even have time to binge-watch shows—when would I have time to date? Don't worry, the moment I find a guy who's willing to bring me hot milk tea when I'm working until 3 a.m., I'll let our popcorn crew know so they can bring the tea."

Lin Chuxia couldn't help laughing. She gazed out the window at the city's skyline. The same city, the same business district, but so many different choices in life. Her friends, her allies, the people who used to be her opponents and now her collaborators—they were all running through these buildings.

And she herself was about to place her biggest bet yet on getting that joint lab agreement signed.

---

"I don't agree."

Vice President Wang, a member of Gu Group's real estate division and an old subordinate of Shen Jianguo's, frowned at the projection screen during the internal review meeting for the joint lab proposal. Fourteen executives sat around the table.

Wang was in his early fifties, a weathered veteran of the company's property arm. "StarTech directly competes with us in three business lines. If we share even part of our underlying AI logic with them, who guarantees our core data security? How do we define the gray areas in intellectual property? I recommend the company conduct a thorough investigation before making a decision—and I'd suggest we table this for at least six months."

A red warning flashed in the upper-right corner of Lin Chuxia's vision.

**[Warning: Mission countdown — 13 days. Internal approval delays will result in timeout failure.]**

But she didn't rush to argue. She stood up and flipped her PPT to the next slide.

"Vice President Wang's concerns are completely valid—intellectual property and security are the most sensitive parts of any tech collaboration. That's why, before drafting this proposal, I cross-referenced legal frameworks with President Zhou of Huayuan Capital and three American law firms. The conclusion: the IP sharing agreement for the joint lab can address every issue you just raised at the contractual level."

She clicked to the next slide—a side-by-side comparison of legal clauses she and Gu Moyan had revised multiple times together.

"As for data security—StarTech has agreed that all joint lab infrastructure will be deployed on Gu Group's private cloud. Every data access will be logged and subject to periodic cross-audits by both parties' chief security officers. We're not letting them into our system—we're building a new space, with new rules, starting from zero."

The room was silent for a few seconds.

"Who's overseeing the entire process?"

"I am," Lin Chuxia said.

Vice President Wang didn't press further. But as Lin Chuxia watched his back disappear through the conference room door, she sensed something more complicated than opposition in his posture—not disagreement, but reluctance. He'd spent twenty-five years in Gu Group's real estate division and had never seen a twenty-six-year-old female strategic advisor push tech-related initiatives on his turf.

After the review meeting, Lin Chuxia went to the break room to grab coffee and ran into an old acquaintance—Shen Jiajia. Since Old Master Gu had made his position clear at the board meeting, Shen Jiajia had lost her edge. She stood by the coffee machine, watching the black liquid drip into her cup, still wearing that sparkling rhinestone hair clip. But her words were nothing like before.

"About the IP clauses—my cousin asked me to tell you she's grateful you didn't pursue legal action over her previous data access."

"Is your cousin doing okay?"

"She quit smoking. She's teaching kids at a charity foundation in Yunnan now. She mailed you a postcard—should be on your desk tomorrow."

Late that night, when Lin Chuxia finally left the office after overtime, she saw the LED display outside Gu Group's main entrance scrolling through the data logic she'd presented at the meeting. The city was even brighter at night than during the day—everyone burning their own light.

---

**Chapter 44: The First Day of the Joint Lab**

Friday, 10 a.m. The joint lab’s unveiling took place at the newly completed Star Tech R&D center.

The plaque was mounted on an inconspicuous side of the building—no ribbon-cutting, no champagne, no red carpet. Lu Ziang had a small brass nameplate installed where the two company logos sat side by side. Engraved on it was a single line: "Joint Research Lab, Gu Group & Star Tech. For those who build."

Gu Moyan didn’t take the stage. Instead, he stood in front of the plaque after it was mounted, tapped it twice with his knuckles—soft but solid.

Then he turned to Lu Ziang and said one thing.

"You’re the first person who’s made me feel like competition is about moving forward, not running around the other."

Lu Ziang smiled and adjusted his wire-rimmed glasses. "I just don’t want to waste good technology. Collaboration doesn’t mean we stop competing—it means we take the competition to a higher level. From fighting over a slice of cake to building a bigger oven."

Gu Moyan didn’t smile, but he extended his hand. The two men who had faced off in board meetings, staked out territory across a hotpot table, and traded invisible strokes on old papers years ago shook hands—a formal gesture, right in front of every team member.

The lab’s permanent research lead was a man named Chen Moyan—a thirty-five-year-old engineering PhD with messy hair, wearing a plaid shirt that was faded but clean. His resume was stellar: six years as a postdoc at Princeton University, lured back by Lu Ziang with the promise, "I’ll cover you—do whatever you want in the lab."

"Miss Lin—we’ve received the industry-side requirements from President Gu’s team. I can have an initial alignment proposal out by this afternoon." He spoke without looking at anyone, but every word was precise.

"Dr. Chen, can I ask you something?"

"Mm." He flipped through papers, a short reply.

"You had great research conditions at Princeton—why come back?"

"Princeton’s research was for someone else. What I do here is for China." He lifted his head and met her eyes—his expression completely different from his usual apathy.

Lin Chuxia suddenly understood why Lu Ziang had signed this man so fast. To persuade an engineer with a sense of purpose, you don’t talk money. You give him a research direction worth dedicating his life to.

At 3 p.m., she received a CCed email from Lu Ziang. Subject: "Joint Lab IP Sharing Terms — Final Draft." She scrolled to the last page—the signature block. Five stamps lined up in a row: Star Tech, Gu Group, Joint Lab Tech Committee Chair, Legal Counsel, and China’s AI Regulatory Office. Forty-eight days of effort, all-nighters, and bureaucratic battles—reduced to five red seals on the last line of pure white A4 paper.

A system window popped up:

【Congratulations, Host, on completing the "Commercial Collaboration Agreement" task. Reward points issued: 600. Current total: 1250. New hidden item unlocked: 'Future Industry Map, Volume 2'—includes a meta-analysis framework for the next three years of industrial trends.

Special milestone reminder: Host current independent favorability score: 58. Only 2 points away from 60.】

---

**Chapter 45: Shen Ruyu's Postcard**

Wednesday morning, a postcard from Yunnan landed on Lin Chuxia's desk.

The front showed a sunset over Erhai Lake—pink-blue sky sliced into layered silk by clouds, the lake reflecting Cangshan's snow. On the back, Shen Ruyu's handwriting:

"This is the first time I painted just for myself. Kids are better than adults. Shen, at Shaxi."

No "I'm sorry." No "Please tell Moyan." No explanation for anything she'd done. Just a child's scribble—a row of stick figures holding hands under a coconut tree, with "Teacher Shen's Class" written at the bottom in watercolor markers.

Zhao Xiaobei had come up to the 42nd floor to grab lunch with Lin Chuxia. She stared at the postcard for a solid ten seconds.

"She's really not coming back to Cloud City?"

"Looks like it." Lin Chuxia stuck the postcard on the whiteboard beside her desk—a board already covered with work notes and a few important photos.

"Will you write back?"

"Yeah. When I'm less busy." Lin Chuxia tucked her pen back into its holder, thoughtful. "She didn't send Moyan a postcard. She sent him that letter from when she was six, and a painting. But for herself—she sent a one-way ticket."

Zhao Xiaobei stared at the Erhai sunset. Her eyes glistened. Then she did what Zhao Xiaobei always did best—summed it up in her own way. "You know, I used to think Shen Ruyu was the textbook definition of a sanctimonious pick-me—the kind of villainess you love to hate. But now? I think she was just trapped in a mold that crushed her into that shape. What she really wanted, all along—"

"—was someone to play with."

They both fell silent at the same time.

That afternoon, a faint system notification flickered across the screen:

[SIDE CHARACTER: Shen Ruyu. Status: Faded from main plot. Long-term impact: Repair of a key anchor in Gu Moyan's personal memories. Influence value: Positive.]

Lin Chuxia dismissed the alert and glanced at the untouched stack of files on her desk—risk assessment materials, ROI models for the new project, and the lab's Phase 2 expansion plan.

Gu Moyan's birthday was less than a month away. Her mind drifted back to that old noodle shop in the basement, his voice: "I'm afraid you'll disappear too—just like I'm afraid a bowl of noodles will go cold."

Her heart thumped. 55, 56, 57—that number was ticking closer and closer.

She told herself: Just two points. Two more to hit sixty.

---

**Chapter 46: Zhao Xiaobei’s Surprise Attack**

The final viewership numbers for Star Technology’s AI Summit livestream were in: twenty million online, with over six hours on trending lists across all platforms. The “Medical Imaging AI Screening System,” jointly launched by Gu Corporation and Star Technology, made its first public debut—and social media exploded.

And the mastermind behind this viral wave? A New Media Director who’d been with the company less than two months: Zhao Xiaobei.

Medical AI had always been marketed in one of three ways: like a research paper, a corporate press release, or a tech-elite circle-jerk. Zhao Xiaobei didn’t pick any of them. The summit’s most viral moment wasn’t an engineer demonstrating an algorithm—it was a woman from a remote mountain village, a regular housewife who’d been successfully treated thanks to early screening through Star Technology’s AI medical platform. No theatrics, no tears—just a quiet lamp flickering in an ordinary video.

“So your strategy was to strip all the tech halo off AI and show how it changes ordinary people’s lives?” a financial reporter asked her on-site.

Zhao Xiaobei replied, “AI, traditional industries, any technology at all—if it doesn’t make ordinary life a little bit better, what’s the difference between it and a pile of scrap metal?”

The second she finished, the comment feed exploded in three directions: her former coworkers, her current boss, and her best friend.

That little marketing grunt who used to choke under Shen Jiajia’s pressure. That nobody who was just another face in the popcorn gallery. Now she stood in front of the national media. No designer gown—just a white blouse and black wide-leg pants. But everyone watching that livestream remembered what she said. They remembered the look in her eyes: the look of a woman who knew exactly what she was worth.

Right after the press conference, Lu Ziang posted on his feed: “The best investors don’t invest in projects—they invest in people. Betting on Zhao Xiaobei for Star Technology was the smartest call I made all year.”

Gu Moyan reposted it and added: “If your headhunter ever comes near Gu Corporation again, I’ll have security escort him out.”

Lin Chuxia burst out laughing right at her desk when she saw that. She screenshotted it and sent it to Zhao Xiaobei, and the two went off in a flurry of messages:

【Lin Chuxia】: The Alpha CEO used three times more characters than your boss! He’s jealous!
【Zhao Xiaobei】: Jealous? Say that again—jealous of WHAT??
【Lin Chuxia】: He’s jealous of Lu Ziang—not of you. Don’t worry.
【Zhao Xiaobei】: I don’t care—I’m remembering this forever. Gu Moyan publicly defended every person on his team, and I was one of them.

---

**Chapter 47: Seeing Herself in the Mirror**

Late at night, Zhao Xiaobei and Lin Chuxia sat together in the living room of Zhao's new rental apartment. The place was right next to the Xingchen Technology Park, much more spacious than her old shoebox. A south-facing balcony offered a glimpse of the Cloud City river in the distance. Zhao Xiaobei was curled up on the couch in her coral fleece pajamas. The couch was brand new—the tags still dangling off it.

Scattered across the coffee table were old relics from their past: a college photo album, the heels Zhao had worn to her interview at Gu Corporation (the soles scuffed beyond recognition), and a printout of Lin Chuxia's first-day selfie at her desk—her face tight, her eyes screaming "Am I going to survive this place?"

"You remember that picture I sent you? You were in that gray suit, holding coffee at the elevator on the 42nd floor, looking like you were marching to your own execution." Zhao picked up the photo, grinning.

"And you have the nerve to bring that up? Your big pep talk that day was, 'If it doesn't work out, we'll just pack our bags and open a bubble tea shop back home.'"

"Hey, I didn't exactly rocket to the top overnight either. After Shen Jiajia tortured me for six months, I was right here on this couch, crying my eyes out—"

"One time you cried for two straight hours. Dropped the remote control and didn't even notice." Lin picked up the thread.

Zhao Xiaobei burst out laughing—laughed so hard tears spilled from her eyes. Not from sadness. It was the kind of laughter that came from looking at each other and knowing exactly who the other person was.

"Chuxia... can I say something?" Zhao hugged a throw pillow to her chest, dropping her usual goofy grin for once. "From college till now, you've been more than my friend. You're the role model I can actually see. Gu Moyan likes you, Lu Ziang respects you, even Old Master Gu approves of you—and it's not because you have some system or a golden finger. I still don't know why you keep talking about those things."

"It's because when you look at your goal, you never look down at the mud on your shoes." Zhao set the old photo of Lin in the gray suit back in the center of the coffee table, right next to her new coffee cup sleeve.

Lin Chuxia looked at her baby-faced friend. From college to this strange new world, from being bullied to speaking in front of the national media—her best friend had never changed. She had always been the first to see the courage buried deepest in Lin's heart.

"Xiaobei, you're my role model too. You're different from me. You do everything thinking, 'I'll leave a little something for the popcorn gallery.' But you're more loyal than anyone. When people hurt you, you never cry over how they treated you—you only worry about the pressure your friends are under. You're the bravest popcorn gallery member I know."

Zhao Xiaobei covered her face, her ears turning as red as a lobster. "Stop! Stop! If you keep this up, I won't be able to speak at the press conference tomorrow! You're both evil—Gu Moyan stealing my bestie, Lu Ziang dumping all these media gigs on me—"

"So, that thing you said you've been holding in your heart for a long time... what was it?"

Outside the window, Cloud City's midnight sprawled in endless warm yellow lights—just like the night they'd first arrived on this chessboard to start the game over.

Zhao Xiaobei lowered her hands from her face, looked Lin in the eyes, and spoke very slowly.

"The girl who used to have nothing and was afraid of everything... she became this. Standing on the most elite business stage in China, making everyone see her name."

---

**Chapter 48: The 'Heart' Clause of the Performance Agreement**

Two weeks into the official launch of the joint lab, Lu Ziang sat in Star Tech's conference room, flipping through the latest financial model from the Gu Corporation partnership with his advisory team and investor reps. Every metric was beating projections—but today's meeting wasn't about revenue forecasts. It was about one very special clause.

Lin Chuxia, Gu Moyan, Lu Ziang, and representatives from three venture capital firms gathered around a small round table. On the table beside each person lay an identical draft of the performance agreement—with two pages that Lin Chuxia and Gu Moyan had finalized only last night.

"If I'm understanding this correctly—" Mr. Zhou of Huayuan Capital took off his reading glasses and stared at Article Three. "Gu Corp and Star Tech have set up a reallocation clause for equity incentives in your three-year joint incubation plan. You two are betting that this investment will produce returns more than three times what either of you could achieve alone. This looks nothing like the standard performance agreements I've seen in any other investment case—"

Standard performance agreements bet on milestones between the project and the money: hitting deadlines, hitting stock price targets. After signing, both sides guarded against each other's audits. But the clause Lin Chuxia had drafted completely flipped the script—turning the 'bet' from defense into sharing.

Each side kept a baseline profit threshold as an exit mechanism. Everything above that got redistributed based on contribution scores—three categories: Gu Corp's real estate channels, Star Tech's AI technology, and the joint lab's talent team. Then Lin Chuxia added one more thing: a periodic reviewer system—an independent third-party project review committee made up of retired industry veterans recommended by both sides. They wouldn't take dividends or manage day-to-day operations. They'd simply conduct a public, non-profit inquiry before every major decision.

"The essence of this clause is simple," Gu Moyan said. "We don't guard against each other. We vouch for each other."

All the investors fell silent.

Mr. Zhou put his glasses back on—spent a full minute rereading those two pages. Then he looked up at Lin Chuxia, then at Gu Moyan.

"You drafted this, Consultant Lin?"

"Yes."

"Then would you be available to be our organizational structure consultant at Huayuan Capital?"

Lu Ziang laughed beside them—not a corporate laugh, but genuine relief at seeing a famously picky old investor acknowledge a new paradigm in business.

After the meeting broke up, he called Lin Chuxia over. He pulled a scarf from his bag and handed it to her—the one from last winter, when she'd stood in the rain at Houhai helping He Yuwei analyze Shen Ruyu's schemes. She'd shivered from the cold, her neck drawn in. He'd bought this scarf afterward, but had never found the right moment to give it to her.

"Winter's already over," Lin Chuxia said, startled as she took it.

"I know. But this is something I bought a long, long time ago and never had the nerve to give you. Today I finally have the right reason—the clause you created isn't a commercial clause."

Lin Chuxia unwrapped it and held up the gray-blue cashmere scarf.

"Then what is it?"

"It's trust that never went on sale."

---

**Chapter 49**: The Countdown

Late at night, Lin Chuxia sat alone at her desk in the apartment, facing the system interface.

She had just finished showering, her hair still damp. The warm air from the AC brushed the back of her neck. But every one of her senses felt frozen — because on the system panel, a red alert she had never seen before was flashing.

【System Final Mission: Redeeming the Child's Fate — The Ultimate 'Bun in the Oven' Side Quest】

Below the prompt, a detailed list of test results scrolled: her biometrics, hormone levels, and a biological status she had never planned for.

Lin Chuxia had believed she could precisely control every system event, every point of affection gained, every task completed — like she was orchestrating algorithms in a corporate war room, measuring every variable as cleanly as a joint lab experiment.

But she had never calculated on this — fate didn't throw its greatest curveball when her affection score hit 100. It threw it when she was already in love with him, on the most ordinary late-spring night when she least expected it.

The panel flipped through queries and flashed a cascade of life-signal data, leaving her no room to think about anything else. She walked out of the bedroom and stood at the floor-to-ceiling window in the living room. The night was deep; the city lay quiet under streetlights. In the distance, the logo light atop the Gu Corporation building glowed faintly — exactly as it had on the first night she had transmigrated here.

Back then, she had looked at that building and felt it was so silent — so silent that she, a stranger from another world standing there, felt she could be uprooted and snatched away at any moment. Now, standing at the same window, she realized she had already grown deep roots in this soil.

A voice from the system panel behind her continued to remind her — the choice for the final mission would naturally manifest within three months. But she didn't need any more points now — the price of the "Real Heart" in the shop was three thousand points, and when she checked her accumulated total, she saw that after the last task reward was issued, her account had exactly three thousand.

She sat under the desk lamp and pressed the 【Confirm Exchange】 button. The system's confirmation tone and the unlocked final mission prompt merged together on the screen into a single "Completed."

She sank back in her chair and let out a long breath. Outside the window it was three in the morning in Cloud City — the last darkness before the pale dawn. She didn't know what she should say to Gu Moyan first, or how to tell him the complete story of that number that had gone from -20 to today.

Her phone screen lit up. It was a WeChat message from him, sent at 3 AM.

【Gu Moyan】: Can't sleep. Got up to design the fonts for the noodle shop's new sign. Got a minute to take a look? The color of one of the characters is exactly the same as the osmanthus blossoms you had in your hair last time.

She stared at the screen. He was awake at three in the morning — not because he couldn't sleep, but because he wanted to say something to her without packaging it as something that needed a reply.

He said it with a color, just like he had said something with that bowl of pea-and-pork-noodle soup. She clutched her phone, typing and deleting in the input box several times.

Finally, she typed back: 【Sure, I'll take a look in the morning.】

She sent it, then pressed the phone against her chest and collapsed onto the sofa. The yellow light from the floor lamp beside her blurred into the shape of an osmanthus tree before her eyes.

---

**Chapter 50: Everything Starts from That Morning**

Wednesday morning, seven o'clock. Cloud City stirred to life in the pale dawn.

Lin Chuxia stood on the rooftop garden on the 48th floor of the Gu Corporation building, watching the city slowly wake up from its dreams. The morning breeze carried the scent of osmanthus from the old family mansion below, and she held a steaming cup of black coffee in her hands.

Gu Moyan stood beside her, his jacket still untied and his collar loosely open. He spread a hand-drawn sign design across the railing—the old noodle shop was getting a new sign. The words "Mom's Taste" were rearranged with a clean, understated font. One character—the mouth radical in "taste"—he'd colored in with a light orange marker, the shade of osmanthus bloom.

"You said you'd help me take a look. Go ahead now." He glanced at her.

Lin Chuxia studied it carefully for two minutes.

"The color for this character—is that the pen you said looked like osmanthus last time?"

"Mm." He leaned against the railing, watching her focused profile as she scrutinized the drawing, a faint smile on his lips. "Advisor Lin, you now have supreme veto power over my aesthetic taste."

"I don't have veto power. I have reservations. If you make that character osmanthus-colored, you'll have to replace the sign every autumn." She pointed to the bottom-left corner where the signature went. "And you need to leave a very small line here."

"What line?"

She rose on her tiptoes and whispered something in his ear. The morning light spilled from behind her, illuminating his face. He blinked, then looked at her silhouette in the sunlight and nodded very, very seriously.

"All right. But I think you should write it yourself—I'll leave you a brush."

"My brush calligraphy is terrible."

"Doesn't matter. If I'm watching you write, it won't be terrible."

At nine, Lin Chuxia returned to her office. The system panel floated quietly in the void to her left, the final mission status frozen at the confirmation click from that late-night session—no new pop-ups, no countdown warnings, no small robots shaped like penguins or pandas reminding her what to do next.

She navigated to the settings page and hovered her finger over the "Sleep Mode" button for a long time. This little blue panel that had accompanied her from -20 to now, once her lifeline and the only anchor she couldn't afford to lose—she no longer needed it. Not because her affection score had reached 100, but because she no longer needed someone else to define what "being loved" meant.

Last night, tossing on the couch until nearly dawn, she'd finally figured it out: isekai wasn't about sending her to a place identical to her original world. It was about sending her to a city where she was willing to stay, using all the memories of that original world.

Her phone buzzed.

【Gu Moyan】: Seven o'clock at the old noodle shop. Don't work late—your words—starting from today, I don't work late either.

【Lin Chuxia】: Okay.

She placed her phone face down on the desk, opened the window, and let the morning breeze rush into the 42nd-floor office. The curtains fluttered up, and the papers on the desk rustled before settling back down under the weight of the fresh cup of coffee she'd just brewed.

Starting tomorrow—if there were new board meetings, new Shen Ruyu-style challenges, new business gambles to face—she would stand like today, high above this city she loved, facing the osmanthus fragrance and all the uncertainties waiting to be conquered, no longer counting gains and losses.

As long as he was on the other side. As long as her best friend ran ahead to lead the way. As long as the dawn that had been fought through countless dark nights was still willing to shine on everything she had chosen.

The End.
